chunks: Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Yaqoub ibn Yazeed, from Abdu Rabbih ibn Rafi', from Al-Hubab ibn Musa, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Whoever is born in Islam as a free person, he is an Arab; and whoever had a treaty (of manumission) and it was fulfilled in his treaty, he is a slave of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family); and whoever entered Islam willingly, he is an emigrant.

key_terms.حُرّاً: Free person (as opposed to a slave)
key_terms.عَهْدٌ: Treaty or covenant, specifically referring to a deed of manumission
key_terms.مَوْلًى: Mawla, a freed slave or client
key_terms.مُهَاجِرٌ: Muhajir, an emigrant who voluntarily entered Islam

ai.seo_question: What are the three categories of people defined by their entry or birth into Islam in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from Al-Kafi, Imam al-Baqir (AS) delineates the foundational social identities within the early Muslim community, linking legal status to origin: those born free are designated as 'Arab,' manumitted slaves with a covenant are 'Mawla' of the Prophet, and voluntary converts are 'Muhajir.' This classification reflects the historical context of the Prophet's era, where lineage, manumission, and voluntary migration were key determinants of social standing and rights within the nascent Islamic polity.

en.hubeali: H 14574 – Sahl Bin Ziyad, from Yaqoub Bin Yazeed, from Abdu Rabbahu Bin Raf’e Al-Hubaab Bin Musa, who has narrated the following: Abu Ja’farasws said: ‘

The one born in Al-Islam as a free person, so he is an Arab, and the one who had a treaty for him and he kept to it, so he is a slave of the Rasool Allah<sup>saww</sup>, and the one who entered in Al-Islam willingly, so he is an emigrant’.
en.sarwar: 126. Sahl Bin Ziyad, from Yaqoub Bin Yazeed, from Abdu Rabbahu Bin Raf’e Al-Hubaab Bin Musa, who has narrated the following: Abu Ja’far (a.s.) said:
